Thank you, Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, and esteemed colleagues. At this 16th meeting of the UNGGIM, we have had the participation of 78 Member States and a total of 358 participants. So it seems appropriate to let me begin by thanking the Member States, the Bureau, the functional groups, our partners, and all contributors for your continued engagement, commitment, and leadership. Your expertise, collaboration and strategic direction remain essential to the committee's achievements and provide valuable direction to UNST's work on global geospatial information management. I would also like to thank the donors whose generous financial and in-kind contributions in 25-26 have supported our geospatial work at the Secretariat. including through the UN GGCE and the UN GGKIC. Both of these centers are now fully operational and we are making good progress towards establishing the UN Global Geospatial Ecosystem Center of Excellence. Together, the Secretariat and the centers help connect normative guidance with tangible country level outcomes. strengthening the cycle from norm setting to knowledge exchange to country impact and back again in the other direction. Dear colleagues, as we enter the final years of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, I would like to highlight three priorities. First, we must expand the impact of our work where it matters and for whom it matters the most. The global UN IGIF implementation survey confirms that countries understand the importance of Earth observations in advancing national priorities alongside global agendas. As more country action plans are prepared and linked to sustainable development outcomes, our focus becomes sharper. This timely shift from awareness raising to meeting concrete country demand requires us to design our work flexibly around expressed needs, rather than producing immaculate products that will remain on the shelf. Second, we must forge closer and more pragmatic connections across all communities working with data for sustainable development. Stronger engagement across the United Nations system anchors geospatial information in multilateral priorities and serves as a cross-domain force multiplier for capacity development, policy support, and monitoring. Likewise, more systematic integration across statistical and geospatial disciplines is equally important, given their complementarities in implementation, assessment, and reporting. Such engagement will also be essential as we respond to AI and other rapidly changing technologies. Together, these efforts can keep the committee's guidance frameworks and methodologies as living instruments, responsive to technological advances and emerging priorities, but remaining practical and accessible to all countries. Third, we must communicate more strategically. As global deliberations converge towards 2030, we must be present in key discussions, including the high level political forum, the post 2030 agenda, and debates such as those on measures beyond GDP, which tailored messages that are convincing and memorable. Part of our objective here is to create the advocates in the room who will speak for us when we are not there. Most immediately, the third United Nations World Geospatial Information Congress to be held in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia from the 16th to 19th November this year offers an important opportunity to extend our reach well beyond the geospatial community. The Congress will engage policymakers, ministers, development specialists, financing institutions, academia, innovators, researchers, the UN system, and the private sector. Our objective must be not only to showcase geospatial excellence, but also to demonstrate why geospatial information is indispensable for better public policies, stronger public digital infrastructure, better informed investment, and tangible outcomes for people and planet. Let me conclude by noting that recruitment restrictions due to financial constraints in the UN regular budget have made it extremely difficult to fill regular budget vacancies, even as the number of posts has declined across all of the Statistics Division and all of DESA over the past year. The committee is also aware that the extra budgetary resources that have supported travel by participants from developing countries are now close to exhaustion and will be used up by the end of this year. Voluntary contributions can be made through standard instruments and agreements with UNDESA, and my team would be happy to facilitate this process if of interest. Thank you.
